summary: Gives an architectural framework for using MPLS to build packet-switched transport networks, called the MPLS Transport Profile (MPLS-TP). It describes functions such as connection-oriented paths, protection and restoration, and OAM, and covers point-to-point paths. It was produced jointly by the IETF and ITU-T. It is informational.

plainLanguage.summary: A plan for making a flexible packet network act like the old telephone-style networks, with fixed paths, backup routes and built-in health checks.

subtitle: How to build packet networks that run and are managed like traditional transport networks, using a strict subset of MPLS.

tldr.problem: Carriers want the flexibility and cost benefits of packet switching, but with the reliability, fixed connections and built-in monitoring that SONET/SDH and OTN transport networks provide.
tldr.mechanism: The framework defines the MPLS Transport Profile (MPLS-TP): a strict subset of MPLS plus a few additions, carrying client traffic over label switched paths and pseudowires, with in-band OAM, protection switching and optional static provisioning with no dynamic control plane.
tldr.outcome: It is an Informational joint IETF and ITU-T framework for point-to-point transport paths only. It is updated by RFC 6215 and RFC 7274, and the detailed mechanisms live in companion documents.

sections.title: Why MPLS Needs a Transport Profile
sections.content:
Optical transport networks (SONET/SDH and OTN) have given carriers a high benchmark for reliability and operational simplicity. They are strictly connection-oriented, with connections that may be long-lived and provisioned manually, and they offer a high level of availability, quality of service and extensive Operations, Administration, and Maintenance (OAM). Carriers want packet switching's flexibility and cost benefits without losing this operational model.

The RFC sets two objectives for the MPLS Transport Profile (MPLS-TP): let MPLS be deployed in a transport network and operated like existing transport technologies, and let it support packet transport services with a similar degree of predictability. Some needed functions already exist in MPLS and others are additions to the tool-set, which should, wherever possible, also be usable in MPLS networks in general.

The document is a product of a joint IETF and ITU-T effort. Its scope is the common functions for point-to-point transport paths. Point-to-multipoint functions are out of scope.
sections.plainLanguage: Old phone-style networks were very dependable but stiff. Packet networks are bendy but less predictable. MPLS-TP tries to get the best of both.

sections.title: Requirements and Scope
sections.content:
The requirements come from RFC 5654 and others, and this RFC only reminds the reader of them. MPLS-TP must not modify the MPLS forwarding architecture and must be based on existing pseudowire and LSP constructs. Point-to-point LSPs may be unidirectional or bidirectional, and congruent bidirectional LSPs must be possible. MPLS-TP LSPs do not merge with other LSPs.

Forwarding must work solely by switching the MPLS or pseudowire label, with or without a dynamic control plane. With static provisioning there must be no dependency on dynamic routing or signaling. OAM, protection and data forwarding must operate without IP forwarding support.

MPLS-TP is a strict subset of MPLS. Functions that RFC 5654 explicitly excludes are Equal Cost Multi-Path (ECMP), LDP signaling used in a way that creates multipoint-to-point LSPs, and IP forwarding in the data plane. Packet transport services must work without dependence on the client or server layer, keep service levels independent of other clients' load, and hide MPLS-TP addressing and topology from clients.
sections.plainLanguage: The rules say: use the same basic road signs as MPLS, never need a map from the internet to work, and keep each customer's traffic separate from everyone else's.

sections.title: Layers, Roles and Adaptation
sections.content:
An MPLS-TP network has two logical layers. The Transport Service layer faces the Customer Edge (CE) nodes, and each client flow is tied to a single point-to-point Transport Service Instance between an ingress and egress Provider Edge (PE). The Transport Path layer aggregates those instances over transport paths (LSPs). Only PE nodes need to know about the service layer, while PE and Provider (P) nodes both take part in the path layer.

Client traffic reaches the network by one of two native service adaptation mechanisms: a pseudowire (PW), which emulates services such as Ethernet, Frame Relay or PPP/HDLC, or an MPLS LSP, which carries network-layer clients such as IP and MPLS-labeled packets. Two interface types are defined at a PE: the User-Network Interface (UNI) toward a CE and the Network-Network Interface (NNI) between PEs in different administrative domains.

The client and server relationship is not marked in the packet. It follows from the network boundary and label context. In the label stack, only one entry may have the S (bottom of stack) bit set to 1.
sections.plainLanguage: Customers hand parcels to a front desk (the edge). The front desk puts each parcel on a labeled truck route, and the trucks along the way only read the route label, not what is inside.

sections.title: Labels, Forwarding and Client Services
sections.content:
MPLS-TP LSPs use the standard label switching and TTL processing of RFC 3031, RFC 3032 and RFC 3443, unchanged. Forwarding is by the label that identifies the transport path, and a label swap is an atomic operation in which the contents after the swapped label are opaque to the forwarder. Only TTL expiry interrupts it. Quality of service uses MPLS Diffserv, and both E-LSP and L-LSP modes are supported.

For pseudowire clients, the stack holds a PW label above the transport LSP label. For network-layer clients, a service LSP label rides on a transport LSP. If several payload types share one service LSP, each needs its own Encapsulation Label. If only one service exists between two PEs, the transport and service labels may be combined into one entry.

Pseudowires may be single-segment or, optionally, multi-segment. Layer 2 and Layer 1 protocols on the attachment circuits are not carried across the network, so the two sides can differ.
sections.plainLanguage: Each parcel gets a stack of stickers. The outer sticker says which truck route to take, and the inner one says which customer it belongs to.

sections.title: OAM, the G-ACh and Return Paths
sections.content:
MPLS-TP OAM covers continuity checks, connectivity verification, performance monitoring, and generating, filtering and managing defect alarms, for sections, LSPs and PWs. It works without a dynamic control plane or IP in the data path, with capabilities equivalent to those in SONET/SDH. If IP is available, existing tools such as LSP Ping, BFD and VCCV may also be used.

The default way to separate OAM packets from user data is the Generic Associated Channel (G-ACh), defined in RFC 5586 and flagged by an Associated Channel Header (ACH) together with a G-ACh Label (GAL). OAM packets share the fate of the data packets. The G-ACh must be used only for channels that are an adjunct to the data service, not as a PW control word alternative. Monitoring is built on Maintenance Entities (MEs), their end points (MEPs) and intermediate points (MIPs), and a MIP can be reached by setting the TTL.

Some protocols need replies. A return path can be in-band, over a bidirectional LSP, or out-of-band, for example over IP routing or a Data Communication Network. The RFC recommends provisioning unidirectional LSPs as associated bidirectional LSPs when an in-band return is needed, and prefers the in-band path on co-routed LSPs.
sections.plainLanguage: Little inspector messages ride along the same track as the cargo, so if the track breaks, the inspectors notice at once. Replies can go back on the same track or by another road.

sections.title: Control, Protection and Management
sections.content:
A dynamic control plane is optional. When used, MPLS-TP uses GMPLS signaling for LSPs and Targeted LDP for pseudowires, consistent with the ASON architecture. LSPs and PWs can also be statically configured, directly or through a management system, independently of each other, and care must be taken to avoid loops. A control-plane failure must not imply failure of existing transport paths.

Survivability schemes include two concurrent paths (1+1), one active and one standby path with guaranteed bandwidth (1:1), and shared protection. They are optimized for linear, ring or meshed topologies, use OAM to detect faults, and can switch without a dynamic control plane. They support revertive and non-revertive behavior.

A Sub-Path Maintenance Element (SPME) is a hierarchical LSP that lets an operator monitor, protect and manage part of an LSP, for example one carrier's portion. Network management covers fault, configuration and performance functions, and at least one standard management protocol such as Netconf, SNMP or CORBA is required for interoperability.
sections.plainLanguage: Paths can be set up by hand or by computers talking to each other. There are spare paths if one fails, and you can put a separate inspector on just one stretch of the road.

layers.label: Client layer
layers.detail: Native service traffic from the CE: network-layer packets or emulated services

layers.label: Transport Service layer
layers.detail: PW or service LSP label identifies the Transport Service Instance; only PEs need it

layers.label: Transport Path layer
layers.detail: Transport LSPs aggregate service instances; PE and P nodes take part

layers.label: Server layer
layers.detail: Carries the MPLS-TP frames and supplies the needed QoS
